item.message: Skill descriptions were shortened to fit the 2% skills context budget. Codex can still see every skill, but some descriptions are shorter. Disable unused skills or plugins to leave more room for the rest.

Validator independence means the automatic checker runs under a separate purpose-specific profile with a","evidence":"`adapters/runtime-adapters/src/harness-executors.mjs` allows direct-inference and Codex CLI profiles to constrain stages, tools, and sandbox access. `docs/13-HARNESS-EXPERIMENTS.md` separates validation, approval, and promotion, while the current architecture says model output cannot authorize itself.","impact":"This determines whether a producer can grade its own work, how many harness profiles every gated stage needs, and whether approval evidence remains credible as workflows and users scale.","question":"How independent must automatic validation be from the harness or model that produced the result?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Separate validator with clean context","consequence":"Every approval gate uses a purpose-specific validator profile that receives only declared artifacts and criteria, improving fault isolation and auditability at the cost of additional runtime and profile maintenance."},{"number":2,"text":"Separate only for high-risk gates","consequence":"Promotion, external delivery, and destructive gates require independent validation, while lower-risk stages may self-check; this reduces cost but introduces a risk-classification policy that must remain accurate."},{"number":3,"text":"Allow producer self-validation","consequence":"The producing harness may also validate before human review, simplifying execution and reducing cost but preserving correlated errors and weaker long-term assurance."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"A clean, purpose-specific validator prevents the same instructions, context, or tool failure from producing and approving an error; manual review then receives stronger evidence without granting the validator authority.","priority":95},{"decision_key":"secure_lan_release_proof","label":"Secure LAN proof","context":"Secure LAN mode means another device on the local network may call NexusCentral only through an encrypted connection and with the shared secret required by both ends. Release proof defines the test that must pass before","evidence":"`packages/central-client/index.mjs` is the shared command boundary for HTTP and WebSocket clients. `services/nexus-node/src/nexus-node.mjs` is the durable host authority, and `docs/12-IMPLEMENTATION-STATUS.md` lists trusted-LAN certificates as unproven.","impact":"This sets the release gate for exposing canonical runs, artifacts, models, and service controls beyond localhost. Weak proof could turn the requested multi-machine API into a credential or evidence exposure path.","question":"What evidence must block release of secure LAN API access?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Real two-device positive and negative proof","consequence":"A physical client must connect with the valid certificate and password, while plaintext, invalid-certificate, and wrong-password attempts must fail; release takes more setup but establishes an enduring security regression gate."},{"number":2,"text":"Single-host network simulation","consequence":"Automated tests exercise certificate and password failures through local network interfaces on one machine; this is easier to repeat but may miss certificate trust, firewall, and device-boundary failures."},{"number":3,"text":"Manual operator checklist","consequence":"Release relies on documented setup and a human connection check; implementation is fastest, but regressions are easier to miss and multi-user support remains harder to certify."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"The risk exists specifically at a device boundary, so one real client-host test plus explicit rejection cases gives meaningful evidence that encryption and authentication fail closed.","priority":93},{"decision_key":"physical_transport_acceptance_topology","label":"Transport acceptance","context":"A physical transport topology is a test using actual NexusCentral and provider processes on separate devices, rather than only simulated nodes. It checks whether one transport-neutral queue behaves consistently across","evidence":"`docs/14-PROVIDERS-AND-PEERJS-ROOMS.md` separates libp2p LAN and PeerJS room transport from routing authority. `kits/jobs-kit/index.mjs` owns leases and retry, while `kits/routing-kit/index.mjs` owns fallback; `docs/12-IMPLEMENTATION-STATUS.md` lists physical mesh scale as unproven.","impact":"This chooses how much real-network evidence is required for the promise that direct, LAN, and PeerJS providers share one reliable queue. It also determines the minimum repeatable hardware acceptance environment.","question":"What physical topology must pass before transport-neutral routing is accepted for production?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Three-node mixed-transport topology","consequence":"A NexusCentral host, a LAN provider, and a PeerJS provider must demonstrate dispatch, atomic lease ownership, disconnect, and fallback; this provides strong cross-transport evidence but requires a maintained multi-device test setup."},{"number":2,"text":"Two-node single-remote topology","consequence":"One host and one remote provider prove basic remote dispatch and disconnect recovery, reducing hardware burden but leaving mixed-transport fallback validated mainly by simulation."},{"number":3,"text":"Simulation remains sufficient","consequence":"Existing scale simulation and local adapter checks gate release, minimizing setup cost but carrying real-network timing, discovery, and disconnect risks into production."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"The central architectural promise is shared behavior across distinct transports; a small three-node topology is the minimum direct proof of that promise and its failure path.","priority":88}]}
